q: Where the fixed overhead absorption rate is set on the basis of normal capacity rather than on the output budgeted for a single period, the volume variance reported in a period of low demand has the merit that it:

options.A: Shows the cost of the capacity left unused as a separate variance, instead of loading that cost into the cost of the units actually produced
options.B: Eliminates the fixed overhead expenditure variance altogether
options.C: Ensures that the fixed overheads are exactly absorbed in every period
options.D: Makes the calendar variance unnecessary in overhead analysis

e: Using a normal capacity absorption rate shows the cost of capacity left unused in low demand as a separate volume variance, instead of loading it onto units produced.

q: The idle time variance in standard costing is always adverse in character because:

options.A: Idle time is valued at the actual wage rate, which is always higher than the standard rate
options.B: Wages are paid for the idle hours although no output is produced in those hours, so that the cost is incurred without any corresponding standard output
options.C: Idle time can arise only through the inefficiency of the workers concerned
options.D: The standard hours allowed for a job never make any provision for normal idle time

e: Idle time variance is always adverse because wages are paid for idle hours while no output is produced in those hours.

q: In a process industry, the material yield variance is correctly computed as:

options.A: The difference between the standard and the actual price of the input, multiplied by the actual input quantity
options.B: The difference between the standard input and the actual input, valued at the actual price of the input
options.C: The difference between the standard yield expected from the actual input and the actual yield obtained, valued at the standard cost per unit of output
options.D: The difference between the budgeted output and the actual output, valued at the selling price per unit

e: Material yield variance = (standard yield from actual input - actual yield) valued at the standard cost per unit of output.

q: Under the marginal costing technique, no fixed overhead volume variance arises in variance analysis because:

options.A: Fixed overheads are treated as a period cost charged in full against the profit of the period, and are not absorbed into the cost of the units produced
options.B: Fixed overheads do not vary at all from period to period in such an enterprise
options.C: The output of the enterprise is always equal to its budgeted output
options.D: Fixed overheads are included in the value of the closing stock under that technique

e: Under marginal costing fixed overheads are a period cost charged in full to the period's profit and are not absorbed into units, so no volume variance arises.

q: The operating statement prepared under standard costing serves its main purpose by:

options.A: Recording the entries to be passed in the financial books of account for the period
options.B: Fixing the selling prices of the products for the following period
options.C: Showing the physical quantities of materials consumed and labour hours worked in the period
options.D: Reconciling the budgeted (or standard) profit with the actual profit of the period through the several variances reported for it

e: The standard costing operating statement reconciles budgeted or standard profit with actual profit through the variances reported for the period.

q: While preparing the schedule of changes in working capital of a trading concern, the accountant records these movements during the year: stock decreased by Rs 24,000, debtors increased by Rs 41,000, prepaid expenses increased by Rs 9,000, bills receivable decreased by Rs 13,000, trade creditors decreased by Rs 18,000, bills payable increased by Rs 11,000 and outstanding expenses increased by Rs 6,000. The net effect of these movements on working capital is:

options.A: A net increase of Rs 31,000
options.D: A net decrease of Rs 3,000

e: Current assets change by -24,000 +41,000 +9,000 -13,000 = +Rs 13,000; current liabilities change by -18,000 +11,000 +6,000 = -Rs 1,000; working capital rises by Rs 14,000.

q: A company keeps its bank overdraft, which is repayable on demand and swings between debit and credit with daily operations, among its current liabilities while preparing the schedule of changes in working capital. During the year this overdraft increased by Rs 55,000, there being no other change. In the schedule, this movement by itself will be shown as:

options.A: An increase in working capital of Rs 55,000
options.B: No change in working capital, an overdraft not being a current liability
options.C: A decrease in working capital of Rs 55,000
options.D: A source of funds of Rs 55,000 in the funds flow statement

e: An overdraft among current liabilities that increases by Rs 55,000 raises current liabilities, so working capital decreases by Rs 55,000 in the schedule.

q: The net profit of a concern for a year is Rs 3,20,000. This profit has been arrived at after charging depreciation of Rs 55,000, preliminary expenses written off of Rs 8,000 and a loss of Rs 12,000 on the sale of furniture, and after crediting a profit of Rs 40,000 on the sale of a plot of land and dividend of Rs 15,000 received on long-term investments. The funds from operations of the concern are:
e: Funds from operations = Rs 3,20,000 + 55,000 + 8,000 + 12,000 - 40,000 - 15,000 = Rs 3,40,000, adding back non-cash and non-operating items.

q: A company treats the provision for taxation appearing in its balance sheet as a current liability for funds flow purposes. Under this treatment, the correct course in preparing the funds flow statement is that:

options.A: The provision made during the year is added back in the adjusted profit and loss account and the tax actually paid is shown as an application of funds
options.B: Both the provision made and the tax paid are shown as applications of funds
options.C: The provision made during the year is shown as a source of funds
options.D: Neither the provision made during the year nor the tax paid during the year is shown separately in the funds flow statement, their effect being absorbed in the change in working capital

e: If tax provision is treated as a current liability, neither the provision made nor tax paid is shown separately; the effect is absorbed in the change in working capital.

q: In the books of a company, the provision for taxation stood at Rs 48,000 at the beginning of a year and at Rs 62,000 at its end. A provision of Rs 55,000 was made for taxation during the year out of the profits. Treating the provision as an appropriation item, the amount of tax actually paid during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, is:
e: Tax paid = opening provision Rs 48,000 + provision made Rs 55,000 - closing provision Rs 62,000 = Rs 41,000, shown as an application.

q: The proposed dividend of a company was Rs 36,000 at the commencement of a year and Rs 45,000 at its close. The dividend proposed in respect of the year itself is Rs 52,000. Treating proposed dividend as an appropriation of profits, the dividend actually paid during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, works out to:
e: Dividend paid = opening proposed Rs 36,000 + proposed for the year Rs 52,000 - closing proposed Rs 45,000 = Rs 43,000, an application of funds.

q: A company pays an interim dividend of Rs 25,000 in cash midway through a year and charges it in its profit and loss appropriation account. In the funds flow statement of that year, this payment is correctly dealt with by:

options.A: Showing it as an application of funds, the amount charged being also added back in computing the funds from operations
options.B: Ignoring it altogether, since an interim dividend is not a final dividend
options.C: Showing it as a decrease in working capital in the schedule of changes
options.D: Deducting it from the sale proceeds of investments of the year

e: An interim dividend paid in cash is an application of funds, and the amount charged is added back in computing funds from operations.

q: The balance of the profit and loss account of a concern was Rs 1,10,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 1,65,000 at its end. During the year the account was debited with depreciation of Rs 60,000, a transfer of Rs 30,000 to the general reserve, proposed dividend of Rs 50,000, a provision for taxation of Rs 38,000 and a loss of Rs 10,000 on the sale of plant, and credited with a profit of Rs 18,000 on the sale of investments. The funds from operations for the year are:

During a year a concern purchases goodwill for a cash consideration and also writes off a part of the goodwill already standing in its books. In computing the funds from operations and in preparing the funds flow statement, the correct treatment is that:

options.A: Both the purchase and the writing off are ignored, goodwill being an intangible item
options.B: The cash paid for the goodwill purchased is an application of funds, while the amount written off, being a non-cash charge, is added back to the profit
options.C: The amount written off is an application of funds and the purchase is added back to the profit
options.D: The purchase is a source of funds and the writing off reduces the working capital

e: Cash paid to purchase goodwill is an application of funds, while goodwill written off is a non-cash charge added back to profit.

q: The plant and machinery account (at written down value) of a concern shows a balance of Rs 4,80,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 5,60,000 at its end. Depreciation charged for the year is Rs 70,000. A machine having a book value of Rs 50,000 was sold during the year for Rs 65,000. The cost of the plant purchased during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, is:
e: Purchases = closing Rs 5,60,000 + depreciation Rs 70,000 + book value sold Rs 50,000 - opening Rs 4,80,000 = Rs 2,00,000, an application.

q: A company allots equity shares of the face value of Rs 3,00,000 to the vendors of a running business as part of the purchase consideration, no cash passing between the parties. In the funds flow statement of the company, this allotment is:

options.A: Not shown at all, since the transaction involves neither a flow of funds nor a flow of cash
options.B: Shown as a source of funds of Rs 3,00,000
options.C: Shown both as a source and as an application of Rs 3,00,000 each
options.D: Shown as an application of funds of Rs 3,00,000

e: Shares allotted to vendors for a business involve no cash or funds flow, so the allotment is not shown in the funds flow statement.

q: From the summarised balance sheets of a concern, its current assets were Rs 3,90,000 and its current liabilities Rs 2,30,000 at the beginning of a year, and its current assets were Rs 4,55,000 and its current liabilities Rs 2,60,000 at the end of that year. The change in its working capital during the year, as it will appear in the funds flow statement, is:

options.A: An increase of Rs 65,000, shown as a source of funds
options.B: A decrease of Rs 35,000, shown as a source of funds
options.C: An increase of Rs 30,000, shown as an application of funds
options.D: An increase of Rs 35,000, shown as an application of funds

e: Working capital rises from Rs 1,60,000 (3,90,000 - 2,30,000) to Rs 1,95,000 (4,55,000 - 2,60,000), an increase of Rs 35,000 shown as an application.

q: Discount allowed on the issue of debentures is written off by a company to the extent of Rs 18,000 during a year and the amount is charged in arriving at its net profit. In computing the funds from operations, this writing off is dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting Rs 18,000 from the net profit as a non-operating item
options.B: Adding back Rs 18,000 to the net profit, the charge being a non-cash item involving no outflow of funds
options.C: Showing Rs 18,000 as an application of funds in the funds flow statement
options.D: Making no adjustment, the discount being a capital loss outside the funds flow statement

e: Discount on debentures written off is a non-cash charge involving no outflow of funds, so Rs 18,000 is added back to net profit for funds from operations.

q: A concern shows its trade debtors in the balance sheet after deducting the provision for doubtful debts standing against them, and follows this practice at both the beginning and the end of the year. For the schedule of changes in working capital, the correct course is to:

options.A: Show the provision for doubtful debts separately as a current liability of the concern
options.B: Add the provision back to the debtors and show the debtors gross in both years
options.C: Take the debtors at their net figure in both years and give no separate treatment to the provision for doubtful debts
options.D: Treat the increase in the provision as a decrease in working capital

e: Where debtors are shown net of the doubtful debts provision in both years, take debtors at the net figure in both years with no separate treatment of the provision.

q: A manufacturing concern closes a year with a net loss of Rs 28,000. The loss has been arrived at after charging depreciation of Rs 36,000 on its plant and writing off goodwill of Rs 9,000, there being no other non-cash or non-operating item in the account. In the funds flow statement, the position regarding its operations is that:

options.A: There are funds from operations of Rs 17,000
options.B: There are funds lost in operations of Rs 28,000
options.C: There are funds lost in operations of Rs 17,000
options.D: Operations have neither generated nor consumed any funds

e: Funds from operations = net loss Rs -28,000 + depreciation Rs 36,000 + goodwill written off Rs 9,000 = Rs 17,000 generated.

q: A non-banking financial company, whose main business is lending money, pays interest of Rs 2,10,000 on the deposits and borrowings raised by it for its lending operations. In its cash flow statement prepared under AS-3, this interest paid is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Financing activities, interest paid being so classified for every enterprise
options.C: Operating activities, the enterprise being a financial enterprise
options.D: No activity, interest being a non-cash appropriation for such a company

e: For a financial enterprise, interest paid on deposits and borrowings for lending is an operating cash flow under AS-3, as lending is its main business.

q: A manufacturing company receives dividend on the shares of another company held by it as a long-term investment. In its cash flow statement prepared under AS-3, this dividend received is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Investing activities
options.D: Operating activities or financing activities, at the option of the company

e: For a non-financial company, dividend received on long-term investments is an investing cash flow under AS-3.

q: A company following Ind AS 7 pays dividend to its equity shareholders during a year. The classification open to it under Ind AS 7 for this dividend paid is to present it as a cash flow from:

options.A: Investing activities only
options.D: Financing activities, or operating activities where it helps users assess the ability to pay dividends out of operating cash flows, the classification being followed consistently

e: Ind AS 7 allows dividend paid to be shown as financing, or as operating where it helps users assess the ability to pay dividends from operating flows, applied consistently.

q: A non-financial enterprise following Ind AS 7 receives interest on the surplus funds it has placed in bank deposits and inter-corporate loans. For this interest received, Ind AS 7 permits it to be classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities only
options.B: Operating activities or investing activities, the classification chosen being applied consistently from period to period
options.D: Investing activities only, with no other choice

e: Ind AS 7 permits a non-financial enterprise to classify interest received as operating or investing, the choice being applied consistently from period to period.

q: While preparing its cash flow statement, a company is able to identify a sum of income tax paid by it specifically with the capital gain arising on the sale of a building, an investing transaction. Consistently with AS-3, this tax paid is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Investing activities, since it is specifically identifiable with an investing activity
options.B: Operating activities in every case, without exception
options.D: No activity, tax on capital gains being a capital item

e: Tax paid specifically identifiable with an investing transaction, such as capital gain on a building sale, is classified as an investing cash flow under AS-3.

q: At the close of a year, a company has cash in hand and at bank of Rs 90,000 and a bank overdraft of Rs 1,40,000 which is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of the company's cash management, the balance fluctuating between overdrawn and positive from day to day. For the cash flow statement, its cash and cash equivalents at the close are taken as:

options.A: Rs 90,000, the overdraft being shown under financing activities
options.B: Rs 2,30,000, being the total of the cash and the overdraft
options.D: A negative figure of Rs 50,000, the overdraft being deducted from the cash in arriving at cash and cash equivalents

e: A demand overdraft integral to cash management is deducted from cash: Rs 90,000 - Rs 1,40,000 = a negative Rs 50,000 of cash and cash equivalents.

q: The credit sales of a concern for a year are Rs 12,40,000. Its trade debtors were Rs 1,55,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 1,95,000 at its end, and debts amounting to Rs 12,000 were written off as bad during the year. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash received from customers during the year is:
e: Cash from customers = opening debtors Rs 1,55,000 + credit sales Rs 12,40,000 - bad debts Rs 12,000 - closing debtors Rs 1,95,000 = Rs 11,88,000.

q: The operating expenses charged in the profit and loss account of a concern for a year amount to Rs 2,85,000. Outstanding expenses were Rs 22,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 31,000 at its end, while prepaid expenses were Rs 14,000 at the beginning and Rs 9,000 at the end. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash paid in respect of these operating expenses is:
e: Cash paid = Rs 2,85,000 + opening outstanding Rs 22,000 - closing outstanding Rs 31,000 + closing prepaid Rs 9,000 - opening prepaid Rs 14,000 = Rs 2,71,000.

q: The profit before tax of a company for a year is Rs 5,10,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 80,000 and interest on long-term borrowings of Rs 45,000 and after crediting interest income of Rs 25,000 and a profit of Rs 18,000 on the sale of plant. During the year its stock increased by Rs 30,000, its debtors decreased by Rs 22,000 and its creditors decreased by Rs 14,000. Income tax of Rs 1,30,000 was paid during the year. Under the indirect method, the net cash from operating activities is:
e: Operating profit before working capital = 5,10,000 + 80,000 + 45,000 - 25,000 - 18,000 = Rs 5,92,000; less net working capital outflow Rs 22,000 and tax Rs 1,30,000 gives Rs 4,40,000.

q: A company satisfies the holders of its convertible debentures by allotting equity shares to them in full conversion of the debentures, no cash being received or paid in the transaction. In its cash flow statement, this conversion is:

options.A: Shown as an inflow under financing activities
options.B: Shown as an outflow under financing activities
options.C: Shown partly under investing and partly under financing activities
options.D: Excluded from the cash flow statement altogether, being a significant non-cash financing transaction disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements

e: Conversion of debentures into shares involves no cash, so it is excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed elsewhere as a non-cash financing transaction.

q: A company acquires a machine from a vendor and, instead of paying cash, allots its own equity shares to the vendor in full payment of the price. In the cash flow statement of the company, this acquisition is dealt with by:

options.A: Showing the value of the shares as an outflow under investing activities
options.B: Excluding the transaction from the cash flow statement, since no cash has moved, and disclosing it as a non-cash investing and financing transaction elsewhere
options.C: Showing it as an inflow under operating activities
options.D: Netting it against the dividend paid during the year

e: Acquiring a machine by allotting shares involves no cash movement, so it is excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed as a non-cash investing and financing transaction.

q: An Indian company holds a deposit in a foreign currency. At the balance sheet date the deposit is restated at the closing exchange rate and an unrealised exchange gain is credited to the profit and loss account, no amount having been received. In the cash flow statement, this unrealised gain is:

options.A: Shown as an inflow under operating activities
options.B: Shown as an inflow under investing activities
options.C: Not a cash flow at all; the effect of exchange rate changes on cash and cash equivalents held in foreign currency is presented separately at the end of the statement, outside the three activities
options.D: Shown as an inflow under financing activities

e: An unrealised exchange gain is not a cash flow; the effect of exchange rate changes on foreign currency cash is presented separately at the end of the statement.

q: During a year a non-financial company purchases machinery for Rs 3,40,000 and goodwill for Rs 90,000, sells long-term investments for Rs 1,55,000 and receives interest of Rs 22,000 on those investments, which it classifies under AS-3 as an investing receipt. Its net cash flow from investing activities for the year is:

options.A: An outflow of Rs 2,53,000
options.D: An outflow of Rs 4,30,000

e: Investing net = -Rs 3,40,000 - Rs 90,000 + Rs 1,55,000 + Rs 22,000 = an outflow of Rs 2,53,000.

q: During a year a company issues equity shares for cash for Rs 4,00,000 including the securities premium, raises a fresh long-term loan of Rs 1,50,000, repays an earlier loan of Rs 1,20,000, redeems debentures for Rs 2,10,000, pays dividend of Rs 85,000 and pays interest of Rs 36,000 classified by it under AS-3 as a financing outflow. Its net cash flow from financing activities is:

options.A: An outflow of Rs 99,000
options.D: An inflow of Rs 99,000

q: Finding its operating cash balances idle, a company transfers a part of them into treasury bills which qualify as cash equivalents and which it holds purely as a part of its day-to-day cash management. In its cash flow statement, this transfer is:

options.A: Shown as an outflow under investing activities
options.B: Not a cash flow at all, being only a movement between items that together constitute cash and cash equivalents
options.C: Shown as an inflow under financing activities
options.D: Shown as an outflow under operating activities

e: Moving cash into treasury bills that are cash equivalents is only a movement within cash and cash equivalents, so it is not a cash flow at all.

q: The equity share capital of a company was Rs 6,00,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 7,50,000 at its end. During the year the company also issued bonus shares of Rs 60,000 out of its reserves. The amount to be shown as a source of funds on account of the issue of share capital is:
e: Cash share issue = capital increase Rs 1,50,000 - bonus shares Rs 60,000 issued from reserves = Rs 90,000 as a source of funds.

q: A long-term loan account shows a balance of Rs 3,20,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 2,75,000 at its end. A fresh loan of Rs 80,000 was raised during the year and no part of any loan was written off. The amount of loan repaid during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, is:
e: Loan repaid = opening Rs 3,20,000 + fresh loan Rs 80,000 - closing Rs 2,75,000 = Rs 1,25,000, shown as an application.

q: The plant account of a concern, maintained at cost, stands at Rs 9,00,000 at the beginning of a year and at Rs 10,40,000 at its end. During the year a plant which had originally cost Rs 1,20,000 was sold away. The cost of the plant purchased during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, is:
e: Plant purchased = closing Rs 10,40,000 + cost of plant sold Rs 1,20,000 - opening Rs 9,00,000 = Rs 2,60,000, an application.

q: A company treats the provision for taxation as a current liability. The provision stood at Rs 52,000 at the beginning of a year and at Rs 68,000 at its end, and tax of Rs 47,000 was in fact paid in cash during the year. A junior accountant insists that this payment of Rs 47,000 must appear as an application of funds. The correct position is that:

options.A: The payment of Rs 47,000 is shown as an application and the increase of Rs 16,000 in the provision is added back to the profit
options.B: The payment of Rs 47,000 is shown as the only application, the provision balances being ignored
options.C: Both the payment of Rs 47,000 and the provision made for the year are shown as applications
options.D: No separate entry is made for the tax paid; only the net increase of Rs 16,000 in the provision figures in the schedule of changes in working capital, as a decrease in working capital

e: With tax provision treated as a current liability, no separate entry is made for tax paid; only the net increase of Rs 16,000 in the provision figures in the working capital schedule.

q: The balance of the profit and loss account of a company was Rs 85,000 at the commencement of a year and Rs 1,32,000 at its close. During the year the account was charged with depreciation of Rs 42,000, a proposed dividend of Rs 55,000 in respect of the year, an interim dividend actually paid of Rs 20,000 and a transfer of Rs 15,000 to a sinking fund, there being no credit item of a non-operating nature. The funds from operations of the company are:
e: Funds from operations = balance rise Rs 47,000 + depreciation Rs 42,000 + proposed dividend Rs 55,000 + interim dividend Rs 20,000 + sinking fund Rs 15,000 = Rs 1,79,000.

q: On completing the funds flow statement of a concern, the accountant finds that the total of the applications of funds, apart from the change in working capital, exceeds the total of the sources of funds by Rs 72,000. This difference is correctly dealt with by showing:

options.A: Funds lost in operations of Rs 72,000 on the applications side
options.B: A net decrease in working capital of Rs 72,000 on the sources side of the statement
options.C: A net increase in working capital of Rs 72,000 on the applications side
options.D: An error of Rs 72,000 to be carried to a suspense account

e: If applications apart from working capital exceed sources by Rs 72,000, the balancing item is a net decrease in working capital of Rs 72,000 shown on the sources side.

q: An enterprise preparing its cash flow statement under Ind AS 7 considers four possible classifications of items dealt with during the year. The classification that is NOT open to it under Ind AS 7 is the presentation of:

options.A: Interest paid as a cash flow from financing activities
options.B: Dividend paid as a cash flow from operating activities
options.C: Dividend received as a cash flow from financing activities
options.D: Interest received as a cash flow from investing activities

e: Ind AS 7 does not permit dividend received to be presented as a financing cash flow; it may be operating or investing only.

q: A firm whose business is dealing in securities buys and sells shares which it holds for trading purposes, turning them over rapidly in the ordinary course of its business. In its cash flow statement prepared under AS-3, the cash flows on the purchase and sale of these securities are classified as cash flows from:

options.A: Operating activities, the securities being held for dealing or trading purposes
options.D: No activity, dealings in securities being excluded from the statement

e: Securities held for dealing or trading are operating items, so cash flows on their purchase and sale are operating cash flows under AS-3.

q: The factory building and plant of a company are destroyed by fire and the company receives a claim of Rs 5,00,000 from its insurers in settlement of the loss of those fixed assets. In the cash flow statement, this receipt is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, all insurance receipts being operating in nature
options.C: Operating activities, but shown net of the premiums paid during the year
options.D: Investing activities, the claim relating to fixed assets of the company

e: An insurance claim received for destroyed fixed assets relates to investing items, so it is classified as an investing cash flow.

q: The credit purchases of a concern for a year are Rs 8,60,000. Its trade creditors were Rs 92,000 at the beginning of the year and Rs 1,18,000 at its end, and during the year the concern received a discount of Rs 8,000 from its suppliers in settlement of their accounts. In a cash flow statement prepared by the direct method, the cash paid to the suppliers during the year is:
e: Cash to suppliers = opening creditors Rs 92,000 + credit purchases Rs 8,60,000 - discount Rs 8,000 - closing creditors Rs 1,18,000 = Rs 8,26,000.

q: The debentures account of a company shows Rs 5,00,000 at the beginning of a year and Rs 3,60,000 at its end. Fresh debentures of Rs 1,00,000 were issued during the year for cash and no debentures were converted into shares. The amount of debentures redeemed during the year, to be shown as an application of funds, is:
e: Debentures redeemed = opening Rs 5,00,000 + fresh issue Rs 1,00,000 - closing Rs 3,60,000 = Rs 2,40,000, an application of funds.

q: A concern buys a new plant costing Rs 3,80,000 and settles the price partly by handing over its old plant, for which the vendor allows Rs 1,10,000, and partly by paying the balance of Rs 2,70,000 in cash. In the cash flow statement of the concern, the correct treatment of this purchase is to show:

options.A: An investing outflow of Rs 3,80,000 and an investing inflow of Rs 1,10,000
options.B: An investing outflow of Rs 3,80,000, the trade-in being ignored
options.C: No outflow at all, the purchase being a single exchange transaction
options.D: An investing outflow of Rs 2,70,000 only, the portion of the price met by the trade-in allowance being a non-cash element kept out of the statement

e: Only the cash element is a cash flow: show an investing outflow of Rs 2,70,000, keeping the Rs 1,10,000 trade-in portion out as non-cash.

q: A company begins a year with cash and cash equivalents of Rs 68,000. During the year its net cash from operating activities is an inflow of Rs 2,15,000, its net cash from investing activities is an outflow of Rs 3,60,000 and its net cash from financing activities is an inflow of Rs 1,85,000. Its cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year are:

In arriving at the cash generated from operations by the indirect method, a company has charged Rs 18,000 in its profit and loss account towards a long-term provision for employee benefits, no part of which has been paid during the year and the balance of which has correspondingly increased. This charge is dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting Rs 18,000 from the profit, the provision being a liability
options.B: Ignoring it, provisions not being dealt with in a cash flow statement
options.C: Treating it as a cash outflow under financing activities
options.D: Adding it back to the profit, in substance as an increase in an operating liability, since the charge has not resulted in any payment of cash

e: A provision charge with no payment is in substance an increase in an operating liability, so Rs 18,000 is added back to profit in the indirect method.

q: The net profit of a company for a year is Rs 4,15,000, arrived at after charging depreciation of Rs 72,000, a provision for taxation of Rs 95,000, a proposed dividend of Rs 70,000, a transfer of Rs 50,000 to the general reserve and a loss of Rs 15,000 on the sale of plant, and after crediting a profit of Rs 28,000 on the sale of investments and dividend of Rs 12,000 received on investments. Treating both the provision for taxation and the proposed dividend as appropriations of profit, the funds from operations are:
In transport operating costing, 'dead kilometres' (dead mileage) means the kilometres run by a vehicle:

options.A: After the vehicle has been condemned and withdrawn from service
options.B: Without carrying any passenger or load, for example in travelling empty between the garage and the point where the service begins
options.C: In excess of the kilometres authorised in the operating schedule
options.D: On roads on which no fare or freight may lawfully be charged

e: Dead kilometres are kilometres run empty without passengers or load, such as travelling from the garage to the starting point of the service, so they earn nothing yet cost money.

q: Commercial tonne-kilometres, as distinguished from absolute tonne-kilometres, are worked out by:

options.A: Adding together the tonne-kilometres of every individual consignment carried
options.B: Multiplying the load carried on each separate section of a journey by the length of that section and adding the products
options.C: Multiplying the total distance travelled by the load despatched (or the average load), without taking account of the loads picked up and dropped at intermediate points
options.D: Multiplying the number of vehicles employed by the distance run by each vehicle

e: Commercial tonne-kilometres use the load despatched or average load times total distance, ignoring loads picked up and dropped en route, unlike absolute tonne-kilometres added section by section.

q: A transport undertaking incurs a total operating cost of Rs 4,50,000 in a period. Its vehicles run 25,000 kilometres in all, of which 2,500 kilometres are dead (empty) kilometres. The operating cost per effective kilometre is:
e: Effective kilometres = 25,000 - 2,500 = 22,500. Cost per effective km = Rs 4,50,000 / 22,500 = Rs 20.00, dead kilometres being excluded from the service performed.

q: A bus has 40 seats and runs 200 kilometres on a day with an average occupancy of 75 per cent of its seating capacity. The passenger-kilometres performed on that day are:

options.A: 8,000 passenger-kilometres
options.D: 6,000 passenger-kilometres

e: Passengers carried on average = 40 seats x 75% = 30. Passenger-kilometres = 30 x 200 km = 6,000.

q: A passenger transport service incurs a total operating cost of Rs 9,60,000 during a month in which it performs 48,00,000 effective passenger-kilometres. Its operating cost per passenger-kilometre is:
e: Cost per passenger-kilometre = Rs 9,60,000 / 48,00,000 passenger-km = Rs 0.20.

q: In the operating costing of a road transport undertaking, which of the following is a standing charge?

options.A: Diesel and lubricating oil consumed
options.B: Cost of tyres and tubes consumed
options.C: Garage rent for housing the vehicles
options.D: Wages paid strictly in proportion to the kilometres run

e: Garage rent is a standing charge because it is a fixed time-based cost incurred whether vehicles run or not, unlike fuel, tyres or mileage-based wages which vary with running.

q: The daily log sheet (log book) maintained for each vehicle in a transport undertaking is kept primarily in order to record:

options.A: The names of the passengers carried on each trip
options.B: The fares collected from passengers on each trip
options.C: The accidents in which the vehicle has been involved
options.D: The kilometres run, the trips made, the load or passengers carried, the fuel issued and the time lost, so that the service performed and the running costs can be worked out

e: The daily log sheet records kilometres run, trips, load or passengers carried, fuel issued and time lost, providing the data needed to measure service performed and running costs.

q: The standing charges of a transport fleet for a period are Rs 1,80,000, its maintenance charges are Rs 60,000 and its running charges are Rs 3,60,000. The fleet runs 50,000 kilometres during the period. The running cost alone per kilometre is:
e: Running cost per km covers running charges only: Rs 3,60,000 / 50,000 km = Rs 7.20. Standing and maintenance charges are excluded from this figure.

q: A truck carries a load of 8 tonnes over a distance of 150 kilometres and returns empty. The total operating cost of the trip is Rs 18,000. The operating cost per absolute tonne-kilometre is:
e: Absolute tonne-kilometres = 8 tonnes x 150 km = 1,200 (the empty return earns no tonne-km). Cost = Rs 18,000 / 1,200 = Rs 15.00 per tonne-km.

q: Where the life of a transport vehicle is expressed and measured in terms of the total kilometres it is expected to run, its depreciation is appropriately treated in operating costing as:

options.A: A running charge, varying with the kilometres run
options.B: A standing charge, spread evenly over the calendar period
options.C: A maintenance charge, grouped with repairs and renewals
options.D: An item excluded from the operating cost altogether

e: If vehicle life is measured in total kilometres expected to be run, depreciation varies with kilometres run, so it is treated as a running charge, not a fixed time charge.

q: A hospital incurs a total cost of Rs 45,00,000 during a period in which the aggregate stay of its in-patients amounts to 30,000 patient-days. The cost per patient-day is:

options.A: Rs 100
options.D: Rs 150

e: Cost per patient-day = Rs 45,00,000 / 30,000 patient-days = Rs 150, the patient-day being the standard cost unit for a hospital.

q: A hotel incurs a total cost of Rs 36,50,000 during a season in which the rooms occupied aggregate 7,300 room-days. The cost per room-day is:

options.A: Rs 500
options.D: Rs 450

e: Cost per room-day = Rs 36,50,000 / 7,300 room-days = Rs 500, using occupied room-days as the hotel cost unit.

q: In the costing of a hotel, most of whose costs (rent, salaries, insurance, depreciation) continue whether the rooms are let or not, a fall in the occupancy of rooms during a period will cause the cost per occupied room-day to:

options.A: Fall, because fewer guests have to be served
options.B: Remain unchanged, because the total cost is unchanged
options.C: Be worked out afresh on the basis of the rooms available rather than the rooms occupied
options.D: Rise, because much the same total cost has to be spread over a smaller number of occupied room-days

e: Most hotel costs are fixed, so when occupancy falls the same total cost is spread over fewer occupied room-days and the cost per occupied room-day rises.

q: A power house generates 15,00,000 units (kWh) at a total cost of Rs 6,00,000. Of the units generated, 20 per cent are consumed within the works and lost in transmission, so that only the balance are sold. The cost per unit sold is:
e: Units sold = 15,00,000 x 80% = 12,00,000. Cost per unit sold = Rs 6,00,000 / 12,00,000 = Rs 0.50, works use and transmission losses being borne by units sold.

q: In the service costing of a boiler house supplying steam to the departments of a factory, the cost unit ordinarily adopted is the cost:

options.A: Per 1,000 kilograms (or per 1,000 litres of water converted into) steam supplied
options.B: Per worker employed in the boiler house
options.C: Per hour for which the factory remains open
options.D: Per unit of the finished product of the factory

e: A boiler house supplies steam, so its cost unit is the cost per 1,000 kg of steam supplied (or per 1,000 litres of water converted into steam).

q: For a cinema (picture house) run as a service undertaking, the composite cost unit most appropriately used for expressing the cost of the service is the cost:

options.A: Per seat per show
options.C: Per employee engaged in the hall
options.D: Per day on which the hall remains open, irrespective of the shows held

e: A cinema sells seat capacity show by show, so the composite cost unit per seat per show best expresses the cost of the service provided.

q: In a process, the normal loss is stated to be 20 per cent of the output of the process. Expressed as a percentage of the input of the process, this normal loss is:

options.A: 20 per cent
options.D: 12.50 per cent

e: Loss is 20% of output: if output is 100, loss is 20 and input is 120. Loss as percentage of input = 20 / 120 = 16.67%.

q: In a process, 10,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 4,65,000. Normal loss is 10 per cent of the input and the scrap realises Rs 15 per unit. The actual output obtained is 8,700 units. The value of the abnormal loss is:
e: Cost per unit = (Rs 4,65,000 - 1,000 x Rs 15) / 9,000 expected units = Rs 50. Abnormal loss = (9,000 - 8,700) x Rs 50 = Rs 15,000.

q: In a process, 8,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 3,64,000. Normal loss is 10 per cent of the input and the scrap realises Rs 5 per unit. The actual output obtained is 7,350 units. The net amount to be credited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account in respect of the abnormal gain is:
e: Cost per unit = (Rs 3,64,000 - 800 x Rs 5) / 7,200 = Rs 50. Abnormal gain 150 units = Rs 7,500, less scrap forgone 150 x Rs 5 = Rs 750, giving net credit Rs 6,750.

q: Halfway through a period the market price of the scrap arising from the normal loss of a process rises sharply, all other costs remaining the same. The effect on the cost per unit of the good output of the process is that it will:

options.A: Rise, because the scrap has become more valuable
options.B: Remain unchanged, because scrap is not a part of the process cost
options.C: Be transferred in full to the Abnormal Loss Account
options.D: Fall, because a larger scrap realisation is credited to the process account against the same gross process cost

e: Scrap realisation is credited to the process account against the same gross cost, so a higher scrap price reduces the net cost borne by good output and its cost per unit falls.

q: For the purpose of computing equivalent production, the units of abnormal loss arising in a process are treated as:

options.A: Having no equivalent units at all, and are ignored in the computation
options.B: Completed units of output, so that they are included in the equivalent production and valued at the full cost per unit of good output
options.C: Units complete only to the extent of their scrap value
options.D: A part of the closing work-in-progress of the process

e: Abnormal loss units are treated as completed units in equivalent production and valued at the full cost per unit of good output, so their full cost is isolated.

q: In a process, 12,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process during a period and there is no opening work-in-progress. The closing work-in-progress is 3,000 units, which are complete as to materials, 60 per cent complete as to labour and 40 per cent complete as to overheads. The equivalent production in respect of labour is:

options.A: 15,000 units
options.D: 13,200 units

e: Labour equivalent units = 12,000 completed + 3,000 closing WIP x 60% = 12,000 + 1,800 = 13,800 units.

q: In a process, the opening work-in-progress is 1,000 units which are 60 per cent complete in respect of conversion costs. During the period 9,000 units are completed and transferred out, and the closing work-in-progress is 2,000 units which are 50 per cent complete in respect of conversion costs. Under the FIFO method, the equivalent units of conversion cost for the period are:

options.A: 10,000 units
options.D: 9,400 units

e: FIFO conversion units = opening WIP finished 1,000 x 40% = 400, plus 8,000 units started and completed, plus closing WIP 2,000 x 50% = 1,000, totalling 9,400.

q: In a process, the opening work-in-progress is 1,000 units which are 60 per cent complete in respect of conversion costs. During the period 9,000 units are completed and transferred out, and the closing work-in-progress is 2,000 units which are 50 per cent complete in respect of conversion costs. Under the average (weighted average) method, the equivalent units of conversion cost for the period are:

options.A: 10,000 units
options.D: 9,000 units

e: Average method conversion units = 9,000 completed + closing WIP 2,000 x 50% = 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000, opening completion being ignored under averaging.

q: Under the average (weighted average) method of dealing with work-in-progress in process costing, the cost of the opening work-in-progress is:

options.A: Merged with the cost incurred during the current period, and a single average cost per equivalent unit is worked out on the combined cost
options.B: Kept entirely separate, and the output first completed is charged only with the opening cost
options.C: Written off in full to the Costing Profit and Loss Account of the current period
options.D: Ignored, only the cost of the current period being spread over the output

e: Under the average method opening WIP cost is merged with current period cost and one average cost per equivalent unit is computed on the combined total.

q: In a process in which the whole of the material is put into production at the very start, the opening work-in-progress already contains all its material. Under the FIFO method, the equivalent units of material to be worked on during the current period in respect of that opening work-in-progress are:

options.A: Equal to the full number of units in the opening work-in-progress
options.B: Equal to one-half of the units in the opening work-in-progress
options.C: Nil, because the material cost of those units was wholly incurred in the previous period
options.D: Equal to the units in the opening work-in-progress multiplied by their degree of completion for conversion costs

e: Under FIFO, opening WIP already has all its material from the previous period, so current-period material equivalent units for those units are nil.

q: The output of a process is transferred to the next process at cost plus 20 per cent on cost. The closing stock of the receiving process, valued at this transfer price, is Rs 72,000. The unrealised profit contained in this closing stock is:
e: Profit is 20% on cost, so profit in transfer price = 20/120 of Rs 72,000 = Rs 12,000, which is the unrealised profit in the closing stock.

q: Where the processes of a factory transfer their output to one another at prices loaded with profit, a stock reserve (provision for unrealised profit) is created at the end of a period in order to:

options.A: Provide in advance for the profit expected to be earned in the following period
options.B: Meet the selling expenses that will be incurred when the stock is sold
options.C: Increase the value at which the closing stock is shown in the balance sheet
options.D: Eliminate from the closing stock, and from the profit of the period, the profit added on inter-process transfers on goods not yet sold outside the factory

e: A stock reserve removes the inter-process profit loaded into unsold closing stock, so stock is shown at cost and profit is recognised only on outside sales.

q: The stock reserve created in an earlier period against the unrealised profit contained in the opening stock of a process is dealt with, when that stock is consumed and the finished goods are sold outside the factory in the current period, by:

options.A: Releasing (crediting back) the reserve, since the profit it represented has now been realised on the outside sale
options.B: Carrying the reserve forward indefinitely so long as any stock remains in the factory
options.C: Writing the reserve off against the cost of the material issued to the process
options.D: Transferring the reserve to the capital reserve of the enterprise

e: When the opening stock is consumed and the goods are sold outside, the profit formerly reserved is now realised, so the stock reserve is released by crediting it back.

q: Finished stock lying unsold at the end of a period is valued at Rs 1,20,000 at the price at which the last process transferred it, that price carrying a profit of 20 per cent on the transfer price itself. The unrealised profit to be reserved against this finished stock is:
e: Profit is 20% on the transfer price itself, so unrealised profit = 20% x Rs 1,20,000 = Rs 24,000 to be reserved against the finished stock.

q: A drawback of transferring the output of each process to the next at a price based on the market price of the product, instead of at cost, is that:

options.A: No profit can ever be ascertained for any process under such a system
options.B: The transfer price may carry an element of profit (or loss) which does not arise from the working of the receiving process, and stocks have still to be reduced to cost by a reserve for the unrealised profit
options.C: The receiving process is debited with less than the cost incurred on its behalf
options.D: The system can be applied only where there is a single process in the factory

e: Market-based transfer prices import profit or loss not earned by the receiving process, distorting its performance, and stocks still need a reserve to bring them back to cost.

q: Under the survey method (weighted units method) of apportioning joint costs, the joint products are given relative weightages (points) having regard to such factors as:

options.A: The quantity of output, the quality and grade of the product, the selling price and the difficulty or conditions of its production and sale
options.B: The number of workers employed on each product after the split-off point
options.C: The floor area occupied by each product in the godown
options.D: The order in which the products happen to emerge from the process

e: The survey method assigns weightages or points reflecting quantity, quality and grade, selling price and the difficulty or conditions of production and sale of each joint product.

q: A joint cost of Rs 4,00,000 is to be apportioned among joint products A, B and C by the survey (weighted units) method. The outputs and weightages per unit are: A — 4,000 units at 3 points, B — 3,000 units at 2 points and C — 2,000 units at 1 point. The share of joint cost borne by product B is:
e: Total weighted points = 4,000x3 + 3,000x2 + 2,000x1 = 20,000. Product B has 6,000 points, so its share = 6,000/20,000 x Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 1,20,000.

q: A joint cost of Rs 9,00,000 is to be apportioned among joint products A, B and C by the net realisable value method. A can be sold for Rs 6,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 1,00,000; B can be sold for Rs 4,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 50,000; C can be sold for Rs 2,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 50,000. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:

A joint product is sold for Rs 3,00,000. The estimated profit on its sale is 20 per cent of the sales value, its selling and distribution expenses are Rs 30,000 and the cost of its further processing after the split-off point is Rs 60,000. Under the reverse cost method, the share of the joint cost apportioned to this product is:
e: Reverse cost = sales Rs 3,00,000 - estimated profit 20% Rs 60,000 - selling expenses Rs 30,000 - further processing Rs 60,000 = Rs 1,50,000 joint cost share.

q: The joint products of a process have aggregate final sales of Rs 12,00,000 and the total cost (joint cost together with the separable costs of all the products) is Rs 9,00,000. Product A has final sales of Rs 4,00,000 and a separable (further processing) cost of Rs 80,000. Under the constant gross margin method, the share of the joint cost borne by product A is:
e: Overall gross margin = (Rs 12,00,000 - Rs 9,00,000) / Rs 12,00,000 = 25%. A's total cost = Rs 4,00,000 x 75% = Rs 3,00,000; less separable Rs 80,000 gives joint cost Rs 2,20,000.

q: Where a joint product has no market price at the split-off point because it is invariably processed further before it can be sold, the basis most appropriately used for apportioning the joint cost to it is:

options.A: The physical quantity of the product, whatever its value
options.B: An equal share of the joint cost for every joint product
options.C: The cost of the further processing carried out on it
options.D: Its net realisable value, that is, its final sales value less the cost of the further processing (and selling expenses) incurred after the split-off point

e: With no split-off market price, joint cost is apportioned on net realisable value: final sales value less further processing and selling costs after split-off.

q: The physical units method of apportioning joint costs cannot be applied directly, without first converting the outputs to a common measure, when:

options.A: All the joint products are measured in the same unit, such as kilograms
options.B: The joint products emerge in unlike states or units, for example one as a liquid measured in litres and another as a solid measured in kilograms
options.C: The joint cost to be apportioned is a large amount
options.D: The joint products are all sold at the split-off point itself

e: Physical units must share a common measure; they cannot be added or compared directly when one product is in litres and another in kilograms.

q: For a goods transport undertaking whose vehicles carry loads that vary greatly from trip to trip, the cost per vehicle-kilometre is a less satisfactory measure of the cost of the service than the cost per tonne-kilometre, because the cost per vehicle-kilometre:

options.A: Cannot be computed from the records of the undertaking
options.B: Takes account only of the standing charges of the vehicles
options.C: Ignores the load actually carried, so that running a vehicle nearly empty appears just as costly a service as running it fully loaded
options.D: Is expressed in money terms rather than in physical terms

e: Cost per vehicle-kilometre charges the same for an empty and a full vehicle, ignoring load carried, whereas cost per tonne-kilometre reflects the actual transport service performed.

q: In an electricity supply undertaking, the cost per unit (kWh) sold is higher than the cost per unit (kWh) generated at the power house, principally because:

options.A: The units generated are measured at a higher voltage than the units sold
options.B: A part of the units generated is consumed in the works itself and a part is lost in transmission and distribution, so that the generating and supply costs have to be spread over the smaller number of units actually sold
options.C: The cost of generation excludes the standing charges of the power house
options.D: Units sold are billed to consumers at a profit, which raises their cost

e: Part of generation is used in the works and part lost in transmission and distribution, so total cost is spread over fewer units sold, making cost per unit sold higher.

q: The scrap arising from the normal loss of the second of two successive processes realises a much higher price per unit than the scrap of the first process. In the process accounts, this higher scrap value is dealt with by:

options.A: Crediting it to the first process, whose material gave rise to the whole of the production
options.B: Crediting it to the Costing Profit and Loss Account directly, without entering any process account
options.C: Spreading it over both the processes in proportion to their inputs
options.D: Crediting it to the second process account alone, in which the loss arose, thereby reducing the cost of the output of that process

e: Scrap value is credited to the process in which the loss arose, so the higher scrap realisation of the second process reduces only that process's output cost.

q: A profit of 25 per cent on the transfer price, charged on the output transferred from one process to another, is equivalent to a profit on the cost of that output of:

options.A: 20 per cent
options.D: 30 per cent

e: Profit of 25% on transfer price means cost is 75% of price. On cost, profit = 25/75 = 33.33%.

q: In the statement of equivalent production of a process in which an abnormal gain has arisen, the equivalent units represented by the abnormal gain are:

options.A: Deducted from the equivalent production, because those units were not expected to be produced and form no part of the normal output on which the cost per unit is based
options.B: Added a second time to the equivalent production of the good output
options.C: Shown as a part of the closing work-in-progress of the process
options.D: Ignored altogether, the gain having no equivalent units

e: Abnormal gain units are deducted in the statement of equivalent production because expected output was lower; this keeps the cost per unit based on normal expected production.

q: In the costing of a laundry run as a service department of a large establishment, the cost unit most appropriately adopted for expressing the cost of the service is the cost:

options.A: Per worker employed in the laundry
options.B: Per machine installed in the laundry
options.C: Per article (or per kilogram) of clothing washed
options.D: Per day on which the laundry works, irrespective of the work done

e: A laundry's service is measured by work washed, so cost per article or per kilogram of clothing washed is the appropriate cost unit.

q: In the operating costing of a fleet of vehicles owned by an undertaking, the cost per vehicle-kilometre worked out from the operating cost sheet is of direct use to management in deciding whether to:

options.A: Replace the fleet with vehicles of a different make
options.B: Fix the wages of the drivers of the vehicles
options.C: Insure the vehicles against third-party risks
options.D: Continue running its own fleet or instead hire transport from outside carriers, by comparing the cost per kilometre with the hire charges quoted per kilometre

e: The own-fleet cost per vehicle-kilometre can be compared directly with outside carriers' hire charges per kilometre to decide whether to run the fleet or hire transport.

q: In a replacement study, the new asset proposed to take the place of the asset in service is conventionally called the:

options.A: Defender
options.D: Successor asset

e: In replacement terminology the existing asset in service is the defender and the new asset proposed to replace it is conventionally called the challenger.

q: A challenger machine costs Rs 9,60,000. The defender can be sold at once for Rs 1,50,000 against a book value of Rs 1,10,000, the gain being taxed at 25 per cent, and the changeover requires additional working capital of Rs 40,000 at the start. The net initial cash outlay of the replacement is:
e: Net outlay = Rs 9,60,000 - after-tax sale proceeds (Rs 1,50,000 - 25% of Rs 40,000 gain = Rs 1,40,000) + Rs 40,000 working capital = Rs 8,60,000.

q: A replacement is expected to reduce cash operating costs by Rs 2,40,000 a year before tax. Depreciation will rise by Rs 60,000 a year and the tax rate is 30 per cent. The incremental annual cash inflow after tax from the replacement is:
e: After-tax cash inflow = Rs 2,40,000 x 70% + extra depreciation Rs 60,000 x 30% tax shield = Rs 1,68,000 + Rs 18,000 = Rs 1,86,000.

q: The net initial outlay on a machine replacement is Rs 6,00,000. The replacement will yield an incremental cash inflow after tax of Rs 1,70,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years, the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at the cost of capital being 3.791. The Net Present Value of the replacement is:

The present value of all the costs, capital and running, of a machine over its whole life is Rs 9,54,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.180. The equivalent annual cost of the machine is:
e: Equivalent annual cost = present value of total costs / annuity factor = Rs 9,54,000 / 3.180 = Rs 3,00,000 per year.
